analysis.one_liner: Creates a single free online portal for credit reports, scores, disputes, and freezes, and puts credit bureaus under CFPB supervision.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 234-179 on June 29, 2020, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made the three big credit bureaus build one joint website where anyone can see their credit report and score for free, dispute errors, and freeze their credit, with no ads or upselling. It would also require the bureaus to match records more carefully, audit their own reports for accuracy, register publicly with the government, submit to Consumer Financial Protection Bureau supervision, and meet federal data-security standards. The House passed it in June 2020; the Senate never took it up, and it expired.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with a credit file. Today the three nationwide bureaus each run their own systems, and their free portals are wrapped in upsells for paid monitoring products. This bill would force a single no-advertising portal with unlimited free access to reports and scores, one-click disputes and security freezes, disclosure of who pulled your report and why, a government ombudsperson to resolve errors the bureaus won't fix, and the right to go to court to force compliance. It also aims at the accuracy problem directly: bureaus would have to match records more carefully and audit samples of their own reports [S4][S5].

how_it_helps.text: One free portal, jointly run by the bureaus, giving unlimited free access to credit reports, credit scores, disputes, security freezes, and a 24-month list of who accessed your report — with no advertising or marketing offers allowed on it, and no requirement that consumers waive legal rights to use it [S5].

Stronger accuracy rules: bureaus must match all nine digits of a consumer's Social Security number (or full identifying details for those without one) before adding information to a file, and must run periodic audits of samples of their reports for accuracy [S4][S5].

A credit reporting ombudsperson at the CFPB to resolve persistent errors the bureaus fail to fix, plus fuller written answers after a dispute, better staffing and training for reinvestigations, and notice across the other bureaus when information is deleted from one file [S4][S5].

Real teeth: courts could order bureaus to comply with credit report protections and award attorney's fees; consumers would get a free score after certain adverse credit decisions; the CFPB gains explicit statutory authority to supervise credit bureaus and to set data-security rules; a public registry of bureaus would be created; and the GAO would study replacing Social Security numbers as identifiers [S4][S5].

analysis.who_pays: The nationwide credit bureaus — Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion above all — and the lenders and other furnishers who feed them. Bureaus lose advertising revenue from the portal, take on accuracy-matching, auditing, staffing, and dispute-response duties, face CFPB examination for the first time under the bill, and become exposed to court orders and fee awards if they don't comply [S4][S5]. Some compliance costs could reach consumers through prices for bureau services, and the ad ban cuts off a channel the bureaus use to sell monitoring subscriptions.

drawbacks.text: The bill doubles down on Social Security numbers: section 3 requires matching all nine digits before adding information to a file, and a GAO study on replacing SSNs would not change anything for at least two years. Rep. Denver Riggleman's motion to recommit would have struck that section and instead prohibited the use of Social Security numbers as identifiers — the objection being that keeping SSNs at the center of credit matching preserves the main tool of identity thieves. It failed 184-228, with 180 of 197 Republicans voting yes [S8][S7].

A single joint portal holding access to every American's credit data is itself an attractive target for hackers; the bill responds with CFPB data-security rulemaking [S5], but concentrates risk in one doorway, and its protections are only as strong as the CFPB's willingness to enforce them.

Disputes would still be investigated by the same bureaus that made the errors; the ombudsperson and audit requirements add oversight, but they don't take error correction out of industry hands [S4][S5].

Compliance costs fall entirely on the bureaus and furnishers, and some portion would likely be passed on through prices for the services bureaus still sell — the bill gives consumers a free floor, not free everything.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers the balance is clearly positive: free, ad-free access to reports and scores, one-click freezes, a government official to escalate stubborn errors, court enforcement, and accuracy rules aimed at mistakes that cost people loans, apartments, and jobs [S4][S5]. The costs are real but modest by comparison: compliance expenses for the bureaus, a new concentration of consumer data in one portal, and the unresolved SSN problem, which the bill studies rather than fixes [S5]. The bill's main weakness is that it polices the bureaus with the bureaus still doing most of the work.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 234-179, the Senate received it the next day and never voted on it, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill on a party-line 31-24 vote on December 11, 2019, and reported it amended on March 12, 2020 [S7].

On June 29, 2020, the House rejected a Republican motion to recommit — a final-chance amendment offered on the floor — by 184-228, with 180 of 197 Republicans voting yes and 228 of 232 Democrats voting no [S8].
The House then passed the bill 234-179: 231 of 232 Democrats in favor, 3 of 197 Republicans in favor, and the sole Independent opposed [S9].
The Senate received the bill on June 30, 2020, and took no further action before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The nationwide credit bureaus — Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — never had to build the ad-free portal, accept CFPB supervision, or face the new accuracy and security obligations. Senate leadership avoided ever taking a position on the floor.

for.name: Josh Gottheimer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through committee and the floor.

for.name: House Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Held markup in December 2019, ordered the bill reported amended 31-24, and reported it to the House on March 12, 2020.

against.name: 174 of 197 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, and 180 of 197 voted yes on the motion to recommit to rewrite the SSN section.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the House-passed bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

against.name: Denver Riggleman
against.what_they_did: Offered the motion to recommit that would strike the SSN-matching section and prohibit Social Security numbers as identifiers; it failed 184-228.

against.name: Maxine Waters
against.what_they_did: Led the committee that reported the bill; as chair controlled the House side of the process but had no power to compel Senate action.

sides.party_line_note: Passage was nearly unanimous among Democrats (231 of 232) with 3 of 197 Republicans in favor; the earlier motion to recommit split the reverse way, 180 Republicans for and 228 of 232 Democrats against.

industries.industry: Nationwide credit reporting agencies (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion)
industries.note: The bill targets their core business practices: a free, ad-free portal undercuts the upsell pipeline that turns free report access into paid monitoring subscriptions, and accuracy matching, audits, CFPB supervision, data-security rules, and court-enforceable duties all raise costs and legal exposure. Because the Senate never acted, they kept the existing system.

industries.industry: Credit monitoring and identity-theft protection sellers
industries.note: The portal must disclose the differences between their paid products and a free security freeze and may carry no advertising or marketing offers, cutting off the confusion-driven sales channel those products rely on [S5].

industries.industry: Banks, lenders, and other furnishers of credit data
industries.note: They face tighter duties to review and consider new information when responding to disputes and must route adverse-action notices through the bureaus [S5], but accurate data also protects them from lending on bad files.
